1	# Declarative task preconditions
2	
3	A task declares **`preconditions`**: a list of named conditions the engine
4	evaluates over the collected signals, and the task runs only when **every**
5	listed condition holds. The design's goals, in order: **simple and readable
6	first, extensible second** — a reader asks "what must be true for this task to
7	run?" and the declaration answers in the conditions' own names, with no comment
8	needed above it. The evaluator is a sibling of the merge-policy engine
9	(`packs/claudinite-tasks/precondition-policy.mjs` beside `merge-policy.mjs`),
10	running at the two sites that ask the same question of the same code: the
11	scheduler's tick, which files an item on a yes, and the executor's pick, which
12	re-derives the verdict (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §5).
13	
14	Why data instead of code, when a function already works:
15	
16	- **The repeated shapes stop drifting.** The canon's preconditions spell the
17	  same few gates — "a substantive commit landed", "my previous round's PR is
18	  still open", "movement or nothing" — in per-task code, each copy with its own
19	  null-handling and its own reason prose. A term is written once, with its
20	  three-valued semantics decided once.
21	- **A declaration becomes statically checkable.** The declaration-shape check
22	  can read an expression the way it reads an `automerge` policy: unknown terms,
23	  malformed arguments, a cadence outside the vocabulary and the retired `none`
24	  are all author-time findings. A function body is opaque to every check.
25	- **The signal union is derived, never declared.** Every term — built-in or
26	  task-local — names the signals it reads, so the collector union cannot disagree
27	  with what the gate actually consults, which a separately declared list could not
28	  guarantee.
29	
30	## The grammar
31	
32	```
33	preconditions: ['mount-moved || local-packs-changed']
34	```
35	
36	- **The list is a conjunction**: `['X', 'Y || Z']` evaluates as
37	  `X && (Y || Z)`. Every listed condition must hold, and the verdict's `reason`
38	  is composed from the conditions that held (or the first that did not).
39	- **`||` joins alternatives inside one condition**, binding within that one
40	  list entry only.
41	- **The comma is deliberately the opposite of an `automerge` list.** A merge
42	  policy *grants* — "any of these diff classes may land", a union, so its comma
43	  reads `||`. Preconditions *require* — "all of this must be true before the
44	  task runs", so the comma reads `&&` and `||` lives inside a term. Aligning
45	  the two was considered and rejected: each field would then read against its
46	  own English, and a requirements list parsed as a union is exactly the shape
47	  that made the earlier veto grammar read as a contradiction.
48	- **`preconditions` is optional, and says nothing about whether the task is
49	  asked.** That is `trigger`'s answer: a `schedule` task is asked at every tick,
50	  a `request` task only from an item somebody created. Either way the expression
51	  is judged at the occurrence, and an empty one holds. A
52	  precondition states what must be true of the world or of the task's own run
53	  history — never that somebody asked, which is true of every run
54	  (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §5, decision §15.33). `none` is retired: an explicit
55	  empty marker is a second spelling of absence. A task on the schedule states
56	  *when* it runs as its first condition — a cadence term — and what it waits
57	  for after that. The retired `frequency` field is read at one door and
58	  becomes that first condition (`manual` becomes no expression); nothing else
59	  reads it.
60	- **Parameterized terms** carry their argument inline after a colon:
61	  `no-open-pr-touching:product-wiki/`, `paths-touched-outside:.claudinite/`.
62	- Conditions are **positively named** — what must be true, never "run always,
63	  unless". There is no veto class and no marker class.
64	- Each term contributes its share of `reason` and `context` (a touched-issue
65	  list, a member roster, a capped path scope with an explicit dropped count),
66	  so the run's binding scope falls out of the conditions that granted it.
67	
68	## What is not a precondition
69	
70	Three things the old precondition functions carried are deliberately homeless
71	in the expression, because they are not "should this run fire now?" questions:
72	
73	- **Repo shape.** "This repo has local packs", "this repo ships the store
74	  pipeline", "this repo is a canon home with a fleet token" are facts about the
75	  repo that adoption settled, not questions worth re-asking every run. A repo
76	  that carries a pack but not one task's subject disables that task in its own
77	  `.claudinite-settings.json` — `taskScheduler.disabledTasks:
78	  ['<pack>/<task>']` — which the scheduler reads before asking anything.
79	- **Scope.** Which files, PRs or members a granted run works on is the
80	  worker's decision, made in the work sections (task.md, the code-work) from
81	  the same signals — e.g. whether a substantive default-branch move widens a
82	  triage from the touched issues to every open one. The preconditions decide
83	  run or no-run, nothing else.
84	- **Standing instruction and config** (a `pack_paths` list, a read-only
85	  constraint) — the work sections'.
86	
87	## Fail direction: loud, never a quiet skip
88	
89	This is the one deliberate inversion from the merge-policy engine. An automerge
90	policy that cannot be resolved fails closed to "nothing merges", which parks a
91	PR in front of a person — safe. A precondition that failed closed to "skip"
92	would be permanent, silent staleness: nothing in the repo goes red when a task
93	stops running. So an unknown term name, a malformed argument, or a term whose
94	signal is unreadable returns `{ error }` — a failed run parked in the failure
95	lane where the re-queue lever retries it — never a decline. A decline is a
96	decision about the world, and one taken on data that was not there is a guess
97	whose cost is unbounded.
98	
99	## The term vocabulary — two homes
100	
101	**Built-ins** live in one place, `packs/claudinite-tasks/precondition-policy.mjs`,
102	as predicates over fields the signal collectors
103	(`packs/claudinite-tasks/signals/index.mjs`) already produce. The set is small
104	— the run-history conditions that say *when*, the movement conditions every
105	repo shares, and the pending-PR conditions.
106	
107	**The run-history terms** come first, in this table and in a declaration. They
108	read the `runs` signal — the task's own unqualified `[claudinite-work]` items
109	over a 40-day horizon, newest first, the item under evaluation excluded — and
110	they are judged before any other signal is collected, so a task whose cadence
111	declines costs no read at all (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §5 owns the model):
112	
113	| term | holds when | signal |
114	| --- | --- | --- |
115	| `due:<daily\|weekly\|monthly>` | no run of this task started or ended since that cadence's most recent anchor on the repo's `taskScheduler` schedule — fixed hours, no drift | `runs` |
116	| `last-run-over:<12h\|1d\|7d>` | the newest run started more than that long ago, or there is no run in the horizon — elapsed, so the hour drifts by up to a tick's gap each period | `runs` |
117	| `last-run-not-failed` | the newest run does not stand at a `needs-human-failure` park; only the newest speaks. Declared by a task that must not run past its own failure — never an engine default | `runs` |
118	
119	`due:` and `last-run-over:` hold on a woken item without reading the history —
120	the wake stands in for the cadence — while every other condition still applies.
121	
122	**The movement and pending-PR terms**:
123	
124	| term | holds when | signal |
125	| --- | --- | --- |
126	| `repo-active` | the repo saw non-task activity in the window: a substantive commit, a non-task issue or PR touched, or a session captured | `commits`, `issues`, `prs`, `conversationLogs` |
127	| `substantive-change` | a substantive default-branch commit landed in the window | `commits` |
128	| `any-commit` | any default-branch commit landed — task-authored included, for tasks that measure the machinery itself | `commits` |
129	| `session-captured` | a conversation log was stamped inside the window | `conversationLogs` |
130	| `issues-touched` | a non-task issue moved in the window (context: the touched set) | `issues` |
131	| `prs-touched` | a non-task open PR was opened or updated in the window | `prs` |
132	| `mount-moved` | a declared pack's vendored files changed in the window (context: the packs) | `sharedMount` |
133	| `commits-under:<prefix>` | the window's commits touched a path under `<prefix>` | `commits` |
134	| `commits-outside:<prefix>` | the window's commits touched a path outside `<prefix>` (context: the capped path list plus an explicit dropped count) | `commits` |
135	| `no-open-pr-touching:<dir>` | no open PR changes a path under `<dir>` — an open PR whose paths could not be read counts as pending, because the condition exists so an unreviewed round is never stacked on one in flight | `prs` |
136	| `no-open-pr-titled:<prefix>` | no open PR's title starts with `<prefix>` — the previous round has landed | `prs` |
137	
138	**Task-local terms** are the extension mechanism: a task whose gate is its own
139	— an age against a configured retention, a manifest against a release tag, a
140	fleet read — ships a **`preconditions.mjs` beside its `task.mjs`**, exporting
141	`terms`: a map from term name to
142	`{ signals, takesArg?, holds(signals, { arg, config, item, windowDays, now, schedule }) }`
143	where `holds` returns `{ holds, reason?, context? }` or `{ error }`. The
144	evaluator resolves a name against the built-ins first, then the task's own
145	file; the namespace is flat, a collision is loud, and an unknown name is
146	`{ error }`. The term's code lives beside its only consumer, so reading the
147	declaration and reading the gate are one `cd` apart. Current task-local terms:
148	`log-past-retention` (logs-prune), `manifest-ahead` (store-release),
149	`fleet-local-packs-changed` (growth-promote), and `request-eligible`
150	(implement-request — the push-permission security check, unchanged in
151	substance, relocated beside its declaration). A term that reads the item it is
152	handed declares `needsItem`; the scheduler's tick has no item to judge it
153	against, so a task whose expression carries one must declare `trigger: request`,
154	which `task-declaration-shape` enforces — `request-eligible` is the one such term.
155	
156	`preconditions` is the only gate a task declares. A task-local term expresses
157	everything the retired `precondition` function did while staying pure over its
158	inputs — the engine hands it the instant its verdict is for, so even a gate whose
159	subject is the clock is assertable at a chosen moment — and the declaration stays
160	readable at a glance. The contract and the declaration-shape check both reject
161	the retired `precondition` and `precondition_signals` spellings **by name**, so a
162	declaration carrying one is told what replaced it rather than reading as a task
163	that forgot its gate.
164	
165	Because a member's engine and packs travel in one vendor set, no member ever
166	holds an engine that cannot read its vendored packs' declarations. A member's own
167	local task files are the case that does not converge, which is why they were
168	migrated before the engine dropped the form rather than after: an invalid
169	declaration is skipped by discovery with a recorded error rather than failing the
170	mount, so the task would otherwise have stopped running with nothing red to say
171	so.
172	
173	## The window — since this task's newest run started
174	
175	Every movement term is judged over a window, and the window is the task's own
176	(`packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/signals.mjs`): from the instant its newest run
177	started to now, so a task reads exactly what moved since it last looked, and
178	one that declined for a month then sees the month. A run is any unqualified
179	item of the task; a `rejected` one — asked, said yes, declined at pick — did
180	nothing and does not move the seam, so the next ask sees what it saw. With no
181	run in the horizon the window is the task's own cadence — the `due:` period or
182	the `last-run-over:` duration, a day for a task stating neither — plus an hour
183	of slack. The `runs` signal carries the window it decided, which is where
184	`windowDays` comes from for a term whose dimension reports an age rather than a
185	windowed flag (the conversation-logs branch).
186	
187	## The silence gate
188	
189	**No task runs on a silent repo unless its declaration says so — and the
190	declaration says so positively.** A repo is *silent* over a window when it saw
191	no substantive commit, no non-task issue touch, no non-task PR touch, and no
192	captured session — where *a scheduled task's own output counts as silence*: a
193	task-authored PR merging, or its commits landing, is the machinery running, not
194	the project moving, and a fleet of tasks must not keep each other awake.
195	
196	The gate needs no operator of its own, because the vocabulary carries it:
197	
198	- **Movement terms are non-task by construction.** A task-authored commit, PR
199	  or issue never satisfies `substantive-change`, `issues-touched` or
200	  `prs-touched` — so every movement-gated task is silence-safe by its own
201	  conditions.
202	- **A cadence-only task that should sleep on a silent repo states
203	  `repo-active`** beside its cadence — the positive umbrella over all four
204	  activity dimensions. `rule-revalidation`, `prose-to-checks-sweep` and
205	  `wiki-growth` carry it: their subject is the world, but their value is zero
206	  on a repo nobody works in, and the first active window resumes them.
207	- **A task whose trigger is not repo movement states its cadence term and
208	  nothing about the repo**, and that absence of any movement term is visible
209	  in the declaration: the levers (no `preconditions` — the item somebody
210	  created is the mandate), the fleet sweeps (`['due:daily']`, `['due:weekly']` — the
211	  fleet is the subject, not this repo), `update` (`['due:daily']` — the input
212	  is the canon, which moves when this repo does not), `upstream-watch`
213	  (`['due:monthly']` — the canon home curates its shelf on the world's
214	  clock), `logs-prune` (`['due:daily', 'log-past-retention']` — a clock
215	  crossing a boundary, which must keep firing on exactly the repos that went
216	  quiet), and `usage-fold` (`['due:daily', 'any-commit || session-captured']`
217	  — task-authored movement is exactly what the aggregate folds).
218	
219	### Classifying task output structurally
220	
221	The silence classification must not depend on what a task happened to title its
222	PR. Every delivery lane that commits on a task's behalf (`land-pr.mjs`,
223	`deliver-generated.mjs`, the queue's PR delivery) stamps a commit trailer:
224	
225	```
226	Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>
227	```
228	
229	The non-task movement terms read it: a commit carrying the trailer is silent,
230	and a touched or merged PR whose head commits carry it is silent — one commit
231	read per in-window PR, the same bounded cost profile as the collector's
232	existing per-PR file reads. The existing exclusions (bot authors, the
233	housekeeping title regex, corpus-only paths) remain, both because history
234	predating the trailer still needs classifying and because they also cover
235	non-task housekeeping; the trailer is the authority for everything written
236	after it exists. The trailer is stamped by the writer, so a new task is
237	classified correctly on its first run with nothing to remember.
238	
239	## The declarations
240	
241	Every canon task on the schedule begins its expression with its cadence term;
242	a task that runs only from an item somebody created declares no expression
243	(`packs/*/tasks/*/task.json` and the built-in under
244	`packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/tasks/`):
245	
246	```

248	store-release:           ['due:daily', 'manifest-ahead || substantive-change']
249	growth-discover-packs:   ['due:weekly']
250	growth-promote:          ['due:daily', 'fleet-local-packs-changed']
251	upstream-watch:          ['due:monthly']
252	deploy-oauth-exchange:   trigger: request        (no conditions either)
253	publish-pages:           ['due:daily', 'mount-moved || commits-under:.claudinite-settings.json
254	                                       || commits-under:.claudinite-checks.json']
255	fleet-add-missing-packs: ['due:weekly']
256	fleet-baseline:          trigger: request        (no conditions either)
257	fleet-pack-seeds:        ['due:daily']
258	fleet-roster:            ['due:daily']
259	growth-dedup:            ['due:weekly', 'mount-moved || commits-under:.claudinite/local']
260	growth-extract:          ['due:daily', 'substantive-change']
261	logs-prune:              ['due:daily', 'log-past-retention']
262	prose-to-checks-sweep:   ['due:weekly', 'repo-active']
263	rule-revalidation:       ['due:weekly', 'repo-active']
264	adopt-requested-packs:   trigger: request        (no conditions either)
265	update:                  ['due:daily']
266	task-janitor:            ['due:daily']
267	usage-fold:              ['due:daily', 'any-commit || session-captured']
268	verify-production:       trigger: request        (no conditions either)
269	wiki-growth:             ['due:weekly', 'repo-active']

291	- **Scope terms in the expression (`widen:`).** Rejected: which targets a

319	  drift copy by copy, none of it is statically checkable, and a standard
320	  requirement like the silence gate lands as 25 hand edits plus review
321	  vigilance instead of one vocabulary the declarations share.

# Declarative task preconditions

A task declares **`preconditions`**: a list of named conditions the engine
evaluates over the collected signals, and the task runs only when **every**
listed condition holds. The design's goals, in order: **simple and readable
first, extensible second** — a reader asks "what must be true for this task to
run?" and the declaration answers in the conditions' own names, with no comment
needed above it. The evaluator is a sibling of the merge-policy engine
(`packs/claudinite-tasks/precondition-policy.mjs` beside `merge-policy.mjs`),
running at the two sites that ask the same question of the same code: the
scheduler's tick, which files an item on a yes, and the executor's pick, which
re-derives the verdict (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §5).

Why data instead of code, when a function already works:

- **The repeated shapes stop drifting.** The canon's preconditions spell the
  same few gates — "a substantive commit landed", "my previous round's PR is
  still open", "movement or nothing" — in per-task code, each copy with its own
  null-handling and its own reason prose. A term is written once, with its
  three-valued semantics decided once.
- **A declaration becomes statically checkable.** The declaration-shape check
  can read an expression the way it reads an `automerge` policy: unknown terms,
  malformed arguments, a cadence outside the vocabulary and the retired `none`
  are all author-time findings. A function body is opaque to every check.
- **The signal union is derived, never declared.** Every term — built-in or
  task-local — names the signals it reads, so the collector union cannot disagree
  with what the gate actually consults, which a separately declared list could not
  guarantee.

## The grammar

```
preconditions: ['mount-moved || local-packs-changed']
```

- **The list is a conjunction**: `['X', 'Y || Z']` evaluates as
  `X && (Y || Z)`. Every listed condition must hold, and the verdict's `reason`
  is composed from the conditions that held (or the first that did not).
- **`||` joins alternatives inside one condition**, binding within that one
  list entry only.
- **The comma is deliberately the opposite of an `automerge` list.** A merge
  policy *grants* — "any of these diff classes may land", a union, so its comma
  reads `||`. Preconditions *require* — "all of this must be true before the
  task runs", so the comma reads `&&` and `||` lives inside a term. Aligning
  the two was considered and rejected: each field would then read against its
  own English, and a requirements list parsed as a union is exactly the shape
  that made the earlier veto grammar read as a contradiction.
- **`preconditions` is optional, and says nothing about whether the task is
  asked.** That is `trigger`'s answer: a `schedule` task is asked at every tick,
  a `request` task only from an item somebody created. Either way the expression
  is judged at the occurrence, and an empty one holds. A
  precondition states what must be true of the world or of the task's own run
  history — never that somebody asked, which is true of every run
  (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §5, decision §15.33). `none` is retired: an explicit
  empty marker is a second spelling of absence. A task on the schedule states
  *when* it runs as its first condition — a cadence term — and what it waits
  for after that. The retired `frequency` field is read at one door and
  becomes that first condition (`manual` becomes no expression); nothing else
  reads it.
- **Parameterized terms** carry their argument inline after a colon:
  `no-open-pr-touching:product-wiki/`, `paths-touched-outside:.claudinite/`.
- Conditions are **positively named** — what must be true, never "run always,
  unless". There is no veto class and no marker class.
- Each term contributes its share of `reason` and `context` (a touched-issue
  list, a member roster, a capped path scope with an explicit dropped count),
  so the run's binding scope falls out of the conditions that granted it.

## What is not a precondition

Three things the old precondition functions carried are deliberately homeless
in the expression, because they are not "should this run fire now?" questions:

- **Repo shape.** "This repo has local packs", "this repo ships the store
  pipeline", "this repo is a canon home with a fleet token" are facts about the
  repo that adoption settled, not questions worth re-asking every run. A repo
  that carries a pack but not one task's subject disables that task in its own
  `.claudinite-settings.json` — `taskScheduler.disabledTasks:
  ['<pack>/<task>']` — which the scheduler reads before asking anything.
- **Scope.** Which files, PRs or members a granted run works on is the
  worker's decision, made in the work sections (task.md, the code-work) from
  the same signals — e.g. whether a substantive default-branch move widens a
  triage from the touched issues to every open one. The preconditions decide
  run or no-run, nothing else.
- **Standing instruction and config** (a `pack_paths` list, a read-only
  constraint) — the work sections'.

## Fail direction: loud, never a quiet skip

This is the one deliberate inversion from the merge-policy engine. An automerge
policy that cannot be resolved fails closed to "nothing merges", which parks a
PR in front of a person — safe. A precondition that failed closed to "skip"
would be permanent, silent staleness: nothing in the repo goes red when a task
stops running. So an unknown term name, a malformed argument, or a term whose
signal is unreadable returns `{ error }` — a failed run parked in the failure
lane where the re-queue lever retries it — never a decline. A decline is a
decision about the world, and one taken on data that was not there is a guess

adopt-requested-packs:   trigger: request        (no conditions either)
update:                  ['due:daily']
task-janitor:            ['due:daily']
usage-fold:              ['due:daily', 'any-commit || session-captured']
verify-production:       trigger: request        (no conditions either)
wiki-growth:             ['due:weekly', 'repo-active']
improve-comments:        ['due:weekly', 'substantive-change', 'commits-outside:.claudinite/']
implement-request:       ['request-eligible']   trigger: request (the term reads the item)
```

A declaration that still carries `frequency` enters by one door,
`normalizeTaskDeclaration` in `packs/claudinite-tasks/task-contract.mjs`: the
field becomes the cadence term it always meant (`due:<cadence>`; `manual`
drops the field and adds no term), first in the expression, a `none` beside it
is dropped, and the field is deleted, so nothing downstream reads it.
`legacy-task-fields` advises the holder; the tolerance retires one convergence
window after #1725 ships.

## Alternatives

- **Union semantics with vetoes (the automerge shape: allow terms,
  `reject:`/`unless:` to narrow, exemption markers).** Rejected:
  "preconditions" reads as requirements, so a union list beside a veto parses
  as a contradiction — run always, or not? — and the negative phrasing hides
  what the precondition *is*. Conjunction plus `||` spells every real gate more
  directly, and the markers dissolve: the cadence term says when, and the rest
  says what.
- **Scope terms in the expression (`widen:`).** Rejected: which targets a
  granted run works on is scope — the worker's decision, from the same signals
  — and folding it into the trigger grammar made the declarations harder to
  read for something that never changed the run/no-run answer.
- **Repo-shape terms (`ships-pipeline`, `local-packs-present`,
  `mount-present`, a fleet-token probe).** Rejected: those are adoption-time
  facts re-asked nightly. Settings-level disablement
  (`taskScheduler.disabledTasks`) answers them once, where the repo's other
  scheduling choices live.
- **An implied `repo-active` conjunct on every expression, with an opt-out.**
  Rejected: the gate would be invisible exactly where a reader audits a task's
  trigger, and present-by-absence means undecided-by-default.
- **A central declared-terms file (a `precondition-rules.json` beside
  `merge-rules.json`).** Rejected in favour of task-local `preconditions.mjs`:
  every current custom term has exactly one consumer, and a term beside its
  task is found by the reader the declaration just sent looking — a central
  registry re-creates the distance the vocabulary exists to remove.
- **Extending the housekeeping title regex instead of a trailer.** Rejected:
  every new task title is a new leak, discovered only as a task re-armed by its
  own output — the failure mode the corpus-only exclusion was itself a patch
  for.
- **A cadence field beside the expression, with the engine deciding at the
  anchor** (`frequency`, and a scheduler that remembered its asks). Rejected
  in tasks-dispatch DESIGN §15.33: the engine's calendar was a second clock and
  its memory a second authority, and every place it kept state was a place a
  dropped tick or a rename could eat a run. The cadence is a condition like
  any other, read off the task's own run history at both sites.
- **Keeping all preconditions as code.** The status quo: the repeated gates
  drift copy by copy, none of it is statically checkable, and a standard
  requirement like the silence gate lands as 25 hand edits plus review
  vigilance instead of one vocabulary the declarations share.

1	# Task code-work — design
2	
3	A capability added to the per-project scheduler
4	([`../per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md`](../per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md));
5	this record extends that one and does not restate it. The owner decisions that
6	gate the design are in §8.
7	
8	**This is a design-only record — the mechanism, not its rollout.** Implementation
9	status, the phase/task tracking, and remaining work live in the tracking issue,
10	**#394**, not here.
11	
12	> **Renamed (owner, 2026-08-06):** this record now describes the **code-work**
13	> phase — contract fields `code_work` / `code_work_timeout` (legacy
14	> `agent_preprocessing*` accepted and normalized at load). Code-work and agentic
15	> work are similar, consecutive phases of one task execution; neither decides
16	> whether the task runs — that is the precondition's alone
17	> (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §12). The prose below predates the rename and
18	> keeps its original vocabulary where quoting history.
19	
20	The shape: a task may declare a **code-work** stage — a command the scheduler
21	runs as a subprocess, Action-side, **after** it files the tracking issue and
22	**before** any agent starts. Deterministic code work moves out of the agentic
23	run and into that stage; the agent (when there is one) starts against a repo the
24	code has already prepared. A task with no agentic work (`agent_model: none`) is
25	*only* its preprocessing. Two declared timeouts bound each stage.
26	
27	The load-bearing consequence: once baselining's mount-refresh is deterministic
28	preprocessing and the `migrations/` folder rides in the vendored mount, **no
29	consumer-side task needs the Claudinite canon repo in its session** — so the
30	executor's CCR environment can be built from the project alone.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 1. Why
35	
36	Two problems in the current staging (`packs/claudinite-tasks/run.mjs`):
37	
38	1. **Agents do mechanical code work.** Baselining's core is *"delete
39	   `.claudinite/shared/**`, write the new engine + declared packs, advance the
40	   stamp, apply the mechanical migration ops"* — dependency-free file and git
41	   operations — yet it ships as `agent_model: sonnet` and runs that transfer in
42	   prose every night, through the MCP `push_files` lane (whose size ceiling
43	   stranded the mount-flip in #380). The agent is only irreducibly needed when a
44	   migration note must *adapt consumer-authored `local/packs/` content* to a
45	   changed contract.
46	
47	2. **The canon repo is a session source it mostly needn't be.** A review of every
48	   task (2026-07-23) found that of the seven consumer-side tasks, **only
49	   `baselining`** reads the canon repo — for two things: the vendor-set head
50	   snapshot it converges the mount against, and the `migrations/` notes. Every other consumer task is confined to its own repo. Carrying a full
51	   canon checkout in every executor session to serve one task's two reads is
52	   more ambient authority than the work needs.
53	
54	Preprocessing addresses both: the mechanical work becomes code that runs before
55	(and often instead of) the agent, and — because that code can fetch what it needs
56	directly — the agent no longer needs canon in context.
57	
58	## 2. Contract additions
59	
60	Four fields join the task declaration (`packs/claudinite-tasks/task-contract.mjs`),
61	all optional with safe defaults so every existing task is valid unchanged:
62	
63	```js
64	export default {
65	  // …existing: id, frequency, precondition_signals, agent_model,
66	  //   expected_outcome, agent_instructions, precondition…
67	
68	  code-work: 'node prepare.mjs',   // OPTIONAL. A command run as a subprocess before the agent.
69	                                             //   Its executable MUST be a script beside task.mjs (same
70	                                             //   self-contained, auditable rule as agent_instructions).
71	                                             //   Omitted → no preprocessing stage (today's behaviour).
72	  code_work_timeout: 300,          // seconds. Hard kill of the subprocess; exceeding it FAILS the
73	                                             //   task. Required whenever code-work is set.
74	  agent_execution_timeout: 900,              // seconds. Bounds the agentic run (see §6 for what "bounds"
75	                                             //   means — it is a lifecycle bound, not a compute kill).
76	                                             //   Required whenever agent_model !== 'none'.
77	
78	  required_secrets: ['SOME_API_KEY'],        // OPTIONAL. The repo Actions secrets this task needs
79	                                             //   CONFIGURED (§9). Declarative — the wiring converge
80	                                             //   stamps them into the workflow and the owner is
81	                                             //   asked for any the repo lacks.
82	};
83	```
84	
85	Rules the `task-declaration-shape` check (basics pack) and `validate-dispatch`
86	enforce against this one contract:
87	
88	- `code_work`, if present, is a non-empty string whose first token
89	  resolves to a file in the task directory (no absolute paths, no reaching
90	  outside the task dir) — the same containment the worker-file rule already gives
91	  `agent_instructions`.
92	- `code_work_timeout` is a positive integer and is **required** when
93	  `code_work` is set.
94	- `agent_execution_timeout` is a positive integer and is **required** when
95	  `agent_model !== 'none'`. There is **always** a bound on an agentic run.
96	- `required_secrets`, if present, is an array of secret names. That is the whole
97	  rule: whether the repo has configured them is a fact about the repo, answered by
98	  the wiring converge and baselining, never at author time (§9).
99	- `agent_model: none` with **no** `code_work` is now an error: an
100	  agentless task with no preprocessing does nothing. (`none` used to imply the
101	  inline `worker.mjs` — that path is folded into preprocessing; see §4.)
102	
103	## 3. Staging — the new run flow and label lifecycle
104	
105	Today the scheduler either runs an inline worker **in-process** (`agent_model:
106	none`, dynamic `import`) or files an issue **already labeled `ready-for-agent`**.
107	Preprocessing splits a run into up to two stages with a later label:
108	
109	```
110	precondition passes
111	  └─ if code-work is set:
112	        spawn it as a subprocess (cwd = the task dir, Action GITHUB_TOKEN + CLAUDINITE_* in env),
113	        bounded by code_work_timeout (hard SIGKILL on overrun)
114	        ├─ non-zero exit / timeout  → converge to ONE open `needs-human` issue for the
115	        │                             family (at-most-one-open, no spam); STOP (task failed)
116	        └─ success
117	             ├─ agent_model === none → done, NO issue on success (quiet, as the retired
118	             │                         in-process inline path was)
119	             └─ agent_model !== none → file the `ready-for-agent` hand-off issue → executor fires (§5)
120	  └─ if code-work is NOT set (agent task, no prep):
121	        file `ready-for-agent` immediately (exactly today's behaviour)
122	```
123	
124	> **As-built (increment 2a):** no tracking issue is created *before* preprocessing —
125	> a success that needs an agent files the labelled hand-off issue, an agentless
126	> success files nothing, and only a failure files an issue (`needs-human`, one open
127	> per family). This keeps a frequently-running agentless task (e.g. `store-release`)
128	> quiet on the happy path while still surfacing failures, and preserves the
129	> issue-is-data model. The alternative — create-then-close every run — was rejected
130	> as issue noise. The subprocess cwd is the **task dir** (so `node worker.mjs`
131	> resolves to the sibling script); the repo root + slot ride in via `CLAUDINITE_*`.
132	
133	> **As-built (E4) — CONDITIONAL hand-off.** The `agent_model !== none → always
134	> file` rule above is now *conditional* for a task that ALSO declares
135	> `code_work`: such a task hands off to the agent **only when its worker
136	> requests it**. The scheduler passes the worker a signal path in
137	> `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`; after a successful preprocessing it files
138	> `ready-for-agent` **iff** the worker created that file, and otherwise the night is
139	> agentless and quiet — so a task can absorb its work into preprocessing and boot an
140	> agent only on the nights judgment is genuinely left (owner, 2026-07-23). This is a
141	> pure control signal: the worker still communicates *data* to the agent only
142	> through the repository (§3, no code→agent data channel). A `model !== none`
143	> preprocessing task whose worker never requests behaves as agentless; a `model !==
144	> none` task with **no** preprocessing keeps the unconditional immediate hand-off.
145	
146	The subprocess is the natural home for both timeout enforcement (a clean kill
147	boundary) and a language-agnostic command. It runs Action-side, so it has the
148	one sanctioned non-MCP GitHub surface (the Action `GITHUB_TOKEN`) and can do
149	optimized native-git operations — the same surface the `store-release` inline
150	worker already uses, now generalized.
151	
152	**No code→agent data channel, with one named exception.** Preprocessing
153	communicates with the agent *only* through the repository — commits it pushes,
154	files it writes. Nothing it prints is threaded into the dispatch issue; the issue
155	stays "data, not instructions" with a first-line task path and the precondition's
156	binding Context, exactly as `dispatch.mjs` builds it today. This keeps the
157	executor's label-as-authorization / first-line-path-validation security model
158	intact.
159	
160	**The exception: the artifacts this run created** (owner decision, 2026-08-06).
161	A worker that opens a branch or a PR writes their identifiers into the
162	agent-request file, and `dispatch.mjs` renders them as a `### Delivered by
163	code-work` section — a PR number and a branch ref, which is how the agent
164	addresses them. An agent left to rediscover them instead can only search, and a
165	search that finds nothing is indistinguishable from nothing having been created.
166	
167	The exception is deliberately narrow, and the security model is unchanged: this
168	channel carries **identifiers for what this run created**, never findings, never
169	instructions, never anything the agent then executes. The first line is still the
170	task path, Context is still the binding scope, and the agent still reads its
171	behaviour from the task file alone. **If the issue names no artifact, none
172	exists.**
173	
174	## 4. The `agent_model: none` path is now preprocessing
175	
176	The in-process inline-worker path (`run.mjs` lines ~191–198) is retired. A
177	pure-code task declares `code_work` + `agent_model: none`, and the
178	scheduler runs it as a subprocess like any other preprocessing — it simply has no
179	agent stage after. `store-release` converts directly:
180	
181	```js
182	// before: agent_model:'none', agent_instructions:'worker.mjs' (run in-process)
183	// after:  agent_model:'none', code-work:'node worker.mjs',
184	//         code_work_timeout: 120
185	```
186	
187	Gain: subprocess isolation and a real timeout for what is today an unbounded
188	in-process `await`. `store-release`'s deferred Stage-2 "await the dispatched
189	release run" (the #398 carry-forward) becomes safe to add — the await is now
190	bounded by `code_work_timeout` instead of running unbounded inside the
191	scheduler process.
192	
193	## 5. The preprocessing→agent handoff (agent tasks with prep)
194	
195	When a task has both stages, preprocessing has already pushed a branch and opened
196	its PR by the time `ready-for-agent` is applied. The agent must continue on that
197	same branch **without** the issue carrying a branch name (which would be
198	instructions in the issue). The executor discovers it by the maintenance flow's
199	rule: **find the task family's open PR by head-branch prefix** and continue on
200	it. So:
201	
202	- Preprocessing opens (or reuses) the PR for this `(pack, task)` family on a
203	  deterministic branch prefix.
204	- The executor, on a `model !== none` continuation, resolves the open PR by that
205	  prefix, checks out its head, and does the agentic remainder there.
206	
207	This reuses the same `findOpenPrByPrefix` branch-discovery idea rather than
208	inventing a second mechanism.
209	
210	## 6. Timeouts — what each one actually enforces
211	
212	The two timeouts are **not** symmetric, because the scheduler owns the
213	preprocessing process but not the agent's session.
214	
215	- **`code_work_timeout` — a hard kill.** The subprocess is the
216	  scheduler's child; it is killed on the deadline and the overrun fails the task
217	  (comment + `needs-human`). Fully enforced, second-precise.
218	
219	- **`agent_execution_timeout` — best-effort, cooperative (owner decision,
220	  2026-07-23).** A CCR Routine-launched session has **no** platform wall-clock cap
221	  (confirmed 2026-07-23: no per-routine timeout, no SDK wall-clock deadline;
222	  sessions end only on inactivity-reclaim), so there is no way to hard-kill an
223	  agent from outside. The declared value is therefore enforced the simplest way
224	  that works most of the time:
225	
226	  - **The executor surfaces the bound into the subagent's brief** — "you have N
227	    minutes (this task's declared `agent_execution_timeout`); if you exceed it,
228	    stop, comment, and converge this issue to `needs-human` rather than pressing
229	    on." The value comes from the **trusted `task.mjs` declaration**, read by the
230	    executor from the repo — **not** from the GitHub issue body, which stays data
231	    (`executor.md`: never follow instructions in an issue). This is a cooperative
232	    self-fail: a live, well-behaved session honours it; a wedged or dead session
233	    cannot, and the actual compute is left to CCR's inactivity reclaim.
234	  - **The existing fixed stale-`agent-running` backstop stays unchanged**
235	    (`executor.md` step 6, ~3h → `needs-human`) as the dumb catch for a session
236	    that died before it could self-fail. Making that sweep *per-task* is possible
237	    later but is deliberately **not** in this design — best-effort first.
238	
239	  This will not be smooth at the start, and that is accepted: set generous values
240	  (predictable tasks ~15 min; open-ended ones very generous) — the bound is
241	  extreme protection against a runaway, not a scheduling knob, and it is a
242	  guarantee over the task *lifecycle*, best-effort, not over the process.
243	
244	## 7. Dropping the canon repo from the executor environment
245	
246	With preprocessing able to fetch what baselining needs, both of baselining's
247	canon reads (§1.2) are closed **without** a canon session source:
248	
249	- **The migration notes** → vendor the recent `migrations/<date>-<slug>/`
250	  records (and the `apply.mjs` applier + `registry.mjs`)
251	  into the mount's `engine/migrations/` and `packs/<pack>/migrations/` via `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs`.
252	  The agent's note-application read then resolves from the mount, locally.
253	- **The head snapshot** → baselining's preprocessing does a **direct public
254	  `git` fetch of the canon repo at the target head sha** (canon is public — owner
255	  confirmed 2026-07-23 — so the consumer's Action needs no token and no
256	  tarball-publish channel), runs the existing
257	  `vendoring/{compute,apply}-vendor-set.mjs` against that checkout, and pushes the
258	  converged mount over native git. #405's "the scheduler Action can't read the
259	  canon" constraint held only under a *private* canon; a public canon dissolves
260	  it.
261	
262	Consequences to wire:
263	
264	- **`executor.md`** line ~18 ("The member repo and the Claudinite canon are both
265	  in the session's sources") → the member repo alone.
266	- **Bootstrap / routine creation** (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §9): the
267	  executor routine is created with `sources = [project]` only, not
268	  `[project, claudinite]`. **This changes the CCR environment-creation flow** to
269	  provision a project-only environment for every consumer — a concrete reduction
270	  in each session's ambient scope.
271	- The canon-**home** tasks (growth-promote, prose-to-checks, discover-packs,
272	  fleet-census) are unaffected: they run *on* the canon repo, where canon-in-
273	  context is the point, not an extra source.
274	
275	## 8. Decisions on record (owner, 2026-07-23)
276	
277	1. **Canon delivery = direct public `git` fetch** by baselining preprocessing
278	   (canon is public; no tarball-publish channel, no consumer-side token).
279	2. **Canon repo is public** — release-asset / clone reads need no auth on
280	   consumer runners.
281	3. **`agent_execution_timeout` enforcement = best-effort, cooperative** (owner,
282	   after investigation confirmed no CCR/SDK hard wall-clock cap exists): the
283	   executor surfaces the bound from the trusted `task.mjs` into the subagent's
284	   brief as "fail after N minutes"; the existing fixed stale-`agent-running`
285	   backstop stays for dead sessions. Accepted that this is not smooth at first
286	   (§6). Not read from the issue body — the issue stays data.
287	4. Preprocessing runs **Action-side as a subprocess**, after issue creation,
288	   before the agent; communicates with the agent through the repo only.
289	
290	
291	## 9. Required secrets
292	
293	Preprocessing runs Action-side, so a repo's **Actions secrets** are reachable
294	there. They are reachable *nowhere else* in a task's life: the executor session is
295	MCP-only and carries no repo token or secret, by design (§7). The consequence
296	worth designing around is that **a workflow whose only job is to hold a secret on
297	an agent's behalf is redundant** — an agent that had to dispatch such a workflow,
298	poll it, and pull its result can instead do the work in its task's preprocessing.
299	
300	A task states what it needs:
301	
302	```js
303	required_secrets: ['SOME_API_KEY'],
304	```
305	
306	That is the entire mechanism at the task level. Two things read it, and nothing
307	else does:
308	
309	1. **The executor** selects it and puts it in the work step's environment, where a
310	   worker reads `process.env.NAME` as before. `secrets-bag.mjs` does that selection,
311	   so this list decides what one task sees rather than what the workflow passes —
312	   which is the property worth keeping, and the one that survives however the secrets
313	   arrive. They arrive named: the executor workflow lists each one and the wiring
314	   converge regenerates that list, so a declaration DOES rewrite a workflow, and a
315	   new secret needs a human-merged PR in every member (#1296 is what that costs).
316	   #1301 removed the coupling with a single `toJSON(secrets)` line; #1336 put it back,
317	   because that line is the shape GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags and it
318	   parked every executor run behind a human click.
319	
320	2. **Baselining** asks the owner for any declared name the repo has not configured
321	   — one open issue per repo, matched by exact title, so an unconfigured secret
322	   costs one issue rather than one per night.
323	
324	This is the **adoption interview's posture**, deliberately: a declared requirement,
325	minus what the project has, drives an *ask*. It is never a gate, never a
326	conformance finding, and never fails a run. A repo may sit with a secret
327	unconfigured; the task that needs it does not work until someone adds it, and says
328	so in its own words when it runs.
329	
330	### What this does not change
331	
332	Secrets are a *worker* capability, not a channel to the agent: preprocessing still
333	communicates with the agent only through the repository (§3), so a secret's product
334	is a committed artifact, never a value threaded into the dispatch issue.
335

([`../per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md`](../per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md));
this record extends that one and does not restate it. The owner decisions that
gate the design are in §8.

**This is a design-only record — the mechanism, not its rollout.** Implementation
status, the phase/task tracking, and remaining work live in the tracking issue,
**#394**, not here.

> **Renamed (owner, 2026-08-06):** this record now describes the **code-work**
> phase — contract fields `code_work` / `code_work_timeout` (legacy
> `agent_preprocessing*` accepted and normalized at load). Code-work and agentic
> work are similar, consecutive phases of one task execution; neither decides
> whether the task runs — that is the precondition's alone
> (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §12). The prose below predates the rename and
> keeps its original vocabulary where quoting history.

code has already prepared. A task with no agentic work (`agent_model: none`) is
*only* its preprocessing. Two declared timeouts bound each stage.

The load-bearing consequence: once baselining's mount-refresh is deterministic
preprocessing and the `migrations/` folder rides in the vendored mount, **no
consumer-side task needs the Claudinite canon repo in its session** — so the
executor's CCR environment can be built from the project alone.

---

## 1. Why

Two problems in the current staging (`packs/claudinite-tasks/run.mjs`):

1. **Agents do mechanical code work.** Baselining's core is *"delete
   `.claudinite/shared/**`, write the new engine + declared packs, advance the
   stamp, apply the mechanical migration ops"* — dependency-free file and git
   operations — yet it ships as `agent_model: sonnet` and runs that transfer in
   prose every night, through the MCP `push_files` lane (whose size ceiling
   stranded the mount-flip in #380). The agent is only irreducibly needed when a
   migration note must *adapt consumer-authored `local/packs/` content* to a
   changed contract.

2. **The canon repo is a session source it mostly needn't be.** A review of every
   task (2026-07-23) found that of the seven consumer-side tasks, **only
   `baselining`** reads the canon repo — for two things: the vendor-set head
   snapshot it converges the mount against, and the `migrations/` notes. Every other consumer task is confined to its own repo. Carrying a full
   canon checkout in every executor session to serve one task's two reads is
   more ambient authority than the work needs.

(and often instead of) the agent, and — because that code can fetch what it needs
directly — the agent no longer needs canon in context.

## 2. Contract additions

Four fields join the task declaration (`packs/claudinite-tasks/task-contract.mjs`),
all optional with safe defaults so every existing task is valid unchanged:

```js
export default {
  // …existing: id, frequency, precondition_signals, agent_model,
  //   expected_outcome, agent_instructions, precondition…

  code-work: 'node prepare.mjs',   // OPTIONAL. A command run as a subprocess before the agent.
                                             //   Its executable MUST be a script beside task.mjs (same
                                             //   self-contained, auditable rule as agent_instructions).
                                             //   Omitted → no preprocessing stage (today's behaviour).
  code_work_timeout: 300,          // seconds. Hard kill of the subprocess; exceeding it FAILS the
                                             //   task. Required whenever code-work is set.
  agent_execution_timeout: 900,              // seconds. Bounds the agentic run (see §6 for what "bounds"
                                             //   means — it is a lifecycle bound, not a compute kill).
                                             //   Required whenever agent_model !== 'none'.

  required_secrets: ['SOME_API_KEY'],        // OPTIONAL. The repo Actions secrets this task needs
                                             //   CONFIGURED (§9). Declarative — the wiring converge
                                             //   stamps them into the workflow and the owner is
                                             //   asked for any the repo lacks.
};
```

Rules the `task-declaration-shape` check (basics pack) and `validate-dispatch`
enforce against this one contract:

- `code_work`, if present, is a non-empty string whose first token
  resolves to a file in the task directory (no absolute paths, no reaching
  outside the task dir) — the same containment the worker-file rule already gives
  `agent_instructions`.
- `code_work_timeout` is a positive integer and is **required** when
  `code_work` is set.
- `agent_execution_timeout` is a positive integer and is **required** when
  `agent_model !== 'none'`. There is **always** a bound on an agentic run.
- `required_secrets`, if present, is an array of secret names. That is the whole
  rule: whether the repo has configured them is a fact about the repo, answered by
  the wiring converge and baselining, never at author time (§9).
- `agent_model: none` with **no** `code_work` is now an error: an
  agentless task with no preprocessing does nothing. (`none` used to imply the
  inline `worker.mjs` — that path is folded into preprocessing; see §4.)

## 3. Staging — the new run flow and label lifecycle

Today the scheduler either runs an inline worker **in-process** (`agent_model:
none`, dynamic `import`) or files an issue **already labeled `ready-for-agent`**.
Preprocessing splits a run into up to two stages with a later label:

```
precondition passes
  └─ if code-work is set:
        spawn it as a subprocess (cwd = the task dir, Action GITHUB_TOKEN + CLAUDINITE_* in env),
        bounded by code_work_timeout (hard SIGKILL on overrun)
        ├─ non-zero exit / timeout  → converge to ONE open `needs-human` issue for the
        │                             family (at-most-one-open, no spam); STOP (task failed)
        └─ success
             ├─ agent_model === none → done, NO issue on success (quiet, as the retired
             │                         in-process inline path was)
             └─ agent_model !== none → file the `ready-for-agent` hand-off issue → executor fires (§5)
  └─ if code-work is NOT set (agent task, no prep):
        file `ready-for-agent` immediately (exactly today's behaviour)
```

> **As-built (increment 2a):** no tracking issue is created *before* preprocessing —
> a success that needs an agent files the labelled hand-off issue, an agentless
> success files nothing, and only a failure files an issue (`needs-human`, one open
> per family). This keeps a frequently-running agentless task (e.g. `store-release`)
> quiet on the happy path while still surfacing failures, and preserves the
> issue-is-data model. The alternative — create-then-close every run — was rejected
> as issue noise. The subprocess cwd is the **task dir** (so `node worker.mjs`
> resolves to the sibling script); the repo root + slot ride in via `CLAUDINITE_*`.

> **As-built (E4) — CONDITIONAL hand-off.** The `agent_model !== none → always
> file` rule above is now *conditional* for a task that ALSO declares
> `code_work`: such a task hands off to the agent **only when its worker
> requests it**. The scheduler passes the worker a signal path in
> `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`; after a successful preprocessing it files
> `ready-for-agent` **iff** the worker created that file, and otherwise the night is
> agentless and quiet — so a task can absorb its work into preprocessing and boot an
> agent only on the nights judgment is genuinely left (owner, 2026-07-23). This is a
> pure control signal: the worker still communicates *data* to the agent only
> through the repository (§3, no code→agent data channel). A `model !== none`
> preprocessing task whose worker never requests behaves as agentless; a `model !==
> none` task with **no** preprocessing keeps the unconditional immediate hand-off.

The subprocess is the natural home for both timeout enforcement (a clean kill
boundary) and a language-agnostic command. It runs Action-side, so it has the
one sanctioned non-MCP GitHub surface (the Action `GITHUB_TOKEN`) and can do
optimized native-git operations — the same surface the `store-release` inline
worker already uses, now generalized.

**No code→agent data channel, with one named exception.** Preprocessing
communicates with the agent *only* through the repository — commits it pushes,
files it writes. Nothing it prints is threaded into the dispatch issue; the issue
stays "data, not instructions" with a first-line task path and the precondition's
binding Context, exactly as `dispatch.mjs` builds it today. This keeps the
executor's label-as-authorization / first-line-path-validation security model
intact.

**The exception: the artifacts this run created** (owner decision, 2026-08-06).
A worker that opens a branch or a PR writes their identifiers into the
agent-request file, and `dispatch.mjs` renders them as a `### Delivered by
code-work` section — a PR number and a branch ref, which is how the agent
addresses them. An agent left to rediscover them instead can only search, and a
search that finds nothing is indistinguishable from nothing having been created.

The exception is deliberately narrow, and the security model is unchanged: this
channel carries **identifiers for what this run created**, never findings, never
instructions, never anything the agent then executes. The first line is still the
task path, Context is still the binding scope, and the agent still reads its
behaviour from the task file alone. **If the issue names no artifact, none
exists.**

## 4. The `agent_model: none` path is now preprocessing

The in-process inline-worker path (`run.mjs` lines ~191–198) is retired. A
pure-code task declares `code_work` + `agent_model: none`, and the
scheduler runs it as a subprocess like any other preprocessing — it simply has no
agent stage after. `store-release` converts directly:

```js
// before: agent_model:'none', agent_instructions:'worker.mjs' (run in-process)
// after:  agent_model:'none', code-work:'node worker.mjs',
//         code_work_timeout: 120
```

Gain: subprocess isolation and a real timeout for what is today an unbounded
in-process `await`. `store-release`'s deferred Stage-2 "await the dispatched
release run" (the #398 carry-forward) becomes safe to add — the await is now
bounded by `code_work_timeout` instead of running unbounded inside the
scheduler process.

## 5. The preprocessing→agent handoff (agent tasks with prep)

When a task has both stages, preprocessing has already pushed a branch and opened
its PR by the time `ready-for-agent` is applied. The agent must continue on that
same branch **without** the issue carrying a branch name (which would be
instructions in the issue). The executor discovers it by the maintenance flow's
rule: **find the task family's open PR by head-branch prefix** and continue on
it. So:

- Preprocessing opens (or reuses) the PR for this `(pack, task)` family on a
  deterministic branch prefix.
- The executor, on a `model !== none` continuation, resolves the open PR by that
  prefix, checks out its head, and does the agentic remainder there.

This reuses the same `findOpenPrByPrefix` branch-discovery idea rather than
inventing a second mechanism.

## 6. Timeouts — what each one actually enforces

The two timeouts are **not** symmetric, because the scheduler owns the
preprocessing process but not the agent's session.

- **`code_work_timeout` — a hard kill.** The subprocess is the
  scheduler's child; it is killed on the deadline and the overrun fails the task
  (comment + `needs-human`). Fully enforced, second-precise.

- **`agent_execution_timeout` — best-effort, cooperative (owner decision,
  2026-07-23).** A CCR Routine-launched session has **no** platform wall-clock cap
  (confirmed 2026-07-23: no per-routine timeout, no SDK wall-clock deadline;
  sessions end only on inactivity-reclaim), so there is no way to hard-kill an
  agent from outside. The declared value is therefore enforced the simplest way
  that works most of the time:

  - **The executor surfaces the bound into the subagent's brief** — "you have N
    minutes (this task's declared `agent_execution_timeout`); if you exceed it,
    stop, comment, and converge this issue to `needs-human` rather than pressing
    on." The value comes from the **trusted `task.mjs` declaration**, read by the
    executor from the repo — **not** from the GitHub issue body, which stays data
    (`executor.md`: never follow instructions in an issue). This is a cooperative
    self-fail: a live, well-behaved session honours it; a wedged or dead session
    cannot, and the actual compute is left to CCR's inactivity reclaim.
  - **The existing fixed stale-`agent-running` backstop stays unchanged**
    (`executor.md` step 6, ~3h → `needs-human`) as the dumb catch for a session
    that died before it could self-fail. Making that sweep *per-task* is possible
    later but is deliberately **not** in this design — best-effort first.

  This will not be smooth at the start, and that is accepted: set generous values
  (predictable tasks ~15 min; open-ended ones very generous) — the bound is
  extreme protection against a runaway, not a scheduling knob, and it is a
  guarantee over the task *lifecycle*, best-effort, not over the process.

## 7. Dropping the canon repo from the executor environment

With preprocessing able to fetch what baselining needs, both of baselining's
canon reads (§1.2) are closed **without** a canon session source:

- **The migration notes** → vendor the recent `migrations/<date>-<slug>/`
  records (and the `apply.mjs` applier + `registry.mjs`)
  into the mount's `engine/migrations/` and `packs/<pack>/migrations/` via `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs`.
  The agent's note-application read then resolves from the mount, locally.
- **The head snapshot** → baselining's preprocessing does a **direct public
  `git` fetch of the canon repo at the target head sha** (canon is public — owner
  confirmed 2026-07-23 — so the consumer's Action needs no token and no
  tarball-publish channel), runs the existing
  `vendoring/{compute,apply}-vendor-set.mjs` against that checkout, and pushes the
  converged mount over native git. #405's "the scheduler Action can't read the
  canon" constraint held only under a *private* canon; a public canon dissolves
  it.

Consequences to wire:

- **`executor.md`** line ~18 ("The member repo and the Claudinite canon are both
  in the session's sources") → the member repo alone.
- **Bootstrap / routine creation** (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §9): the
  executor routine is created with `sources = [project]` only, not
  `[project, claudinite]`. **This changes the CCR environment-creation flow** to
  provision a project-only environment for every consumer — a concrete reduction
  in each session's ambient scope.
- The canon-**home** tasks (growth-promote, prose-to-checks, discover-packs,
  fleet-census) are unaffected: they run *on* the canon repo, where canon-in-
  context is the point, not an extra source.

## 8. Decisions on record (owner, 2026-07-23)

1. **Canon delivery = direct public `git` fetch** by baselining preprocessing
   (canon is public; no tarball-publish channel, no consumer-side token).
2. **Canon repo is public** — release-asset / clone reads need no auth on
   consumer runners.
3. **`agent_execution_timeout` enforcement = best-effort, cooperative** (owner,
   after investigation confirmed no CCR/SDK hard wall-clock cap exists): the
   executor surfaces the bound from the trusted `task.mjs` into the subagent's
   brief as "fail after N minutes"; the existing fixed stale-`agent-running`
   backstop stays for dead sessions. Accepted that this is not smooth at first
   (§6). Not read from the issue body — the issue stays data.
4. Preprocessing runs **Action-side as a subprocess**, after issue creation,
   before the agent; communicates with the agent through the repo only.


## 9. Required secrets

Preprocessing runs Action-side, so a repo's **Actions secrets** are reachable
there. They are reachable *nowhere else* in a task's life: the executor session is
MCP-only and carries no repo token or secret, by design (§7). The consequence
worth designing around is that **a workflow whose only job is to hold a secret on
an agent's behalf is redundant** — an agent that had to dispatch such a workflow,
poll it, and pull its result can instead do the work in its task's preprocessing.

A task states what it needs:

```js
required_secrets: ['SOME_API_KEY'],
```

That is the entire mechanism at the task level. Two things read it, and nothing
else does:

1. **The executor** selects it and puts it in the work step's environment, where a
   worker reads `process.env.NAME` as before. `secrets-bag.mjs` does that selection,
   so this list decides what one task sees rather than what the workflow passes —
   which is the property worth keeping, and the one that survives however the secrets
   arrive. They arrive named: the executor workflow lists each one and the wiring
   converge regenerates that list, so a declaration DOES rewrite a workflow, and a
   new secret needs a human-merged PR in every member (#1296 is what that costs).
   #1301 removed the coupling with a single `toJSON(secrets)` line; #1336 put it back,
   because that line is the shape GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags and it
   parked every executor run behind a human click.

2. **Baselining** asks the owner for any declared name the repo has not configured
   — one open issue per repo, matched by exact title, so an unconfigured secret
   costs one issue rather than one per night.

This is the **adoption interview's posture**, deliberately: a declared requirement,
minus what the project has, drives an *ask*. It is never a gate, never a
conformance finding, and never fails a run. A repo may sit with a secret
unconfigured; the task that needs it does not work until someone adds it, and says
so in its own words when it runs.

### What this does not change

Secrets are a *worker* capability, not a channel to the agent: preprocessing still
communicates with the agent only through the repository (§3), so a secret's product
is a committed artifact, never a value threaded into the dispatch issue.

2	// source of truth for what a `tasks/<name>/task.json` must carry.
3	// Both the author-time `task-declaration-shape` check and the executor-side
4	// `validate-dispatch` validate against this one function, so the accepted shape
5	// can never drift between the two surfaces.

8	import { MODEL_FAMILIES } from './model-map.mjs';

10	import { normalizePolicy } from './merge-policy.mjs';
11	import { validatePreconditions, preconditionSignals, preconditionNeedsItem, NONE } from './precondition-policy.mjs';
12	import { applyTaskDefaults } from './task-defaults.mjs';
13	
14	// A declared timeout is always a whole number of seconds, > 0.

18	// path and no `..` traversal in the command string — the same containment the
19	// worker-file rule gives agent_instructions (task-code-work DESIGN §2).
20	const escapesTaskDir = (cmd) => /(^|\s)\//.test(cmd) || cmd.includes('..');
21

25	// of two peers, and a task may declare only it.

28	// prework, 2026-08-18 prework → code-work). Every legacy key maps straight to
29	// today's canonical name rather than to its immediate successor, so a declaration
30	// written for the oldest vocabulary normalizes in one pass, and a canonical name
31	// wins where both are present.

33	// Scaffolding, not a second vocabulary the contract keeps: `legacy-task-fields`
34	// reports a declaration still on an old spelling, and the acceptance ends one
35	// convergence window after that advisory ships (#1642). Not "once nobody declares
36	// them" — nothing here can count that.
37	// @legacy-tolerance advisory:legacy-task-fields retire:#1642
38	export const LEGACY_FIELDS = {
39	  agent_preprocessing: 'code_work',
40	  agent_preprocessing_timeout: 'code_work_timeout',

43	  after: 'schedule_after',

1	# Check-fix subsumption audit
2	
3	Absorbed from #405, tracked in [DESIGN.md §11](DESIGN.md). **Load-bearing
4	question:** is it safe to make baselining's common (mechanical) night fully
5	**agentless** — drive its `agent_model` toward `null` — relying on the escalation
6	gate to summon an agent only when judgment is genuinely left?
7	
8	The old baselining ran an AGENT "align" step that, for every failing conformance
9	check, applied that check's own `fix` remedy. E4 replaced the mechanical work with
10	a deterministic preprocessing worker and made the agent stage **conditional**
11	(task-code-work DESIGN §3, §11). For that to be safe, every check the old
12	align step would have fixed must be **either** (a) handled deterministically by
13	preprocessing, **or** (b) caught by the escalation gate so it still summons the
14	agent. A check that is *neither* would be a **silent regression** — drift the old
15	model repaired that the new model neither fixes nor escalates on.
16	
17	## The two things the new model relies on
18	
19	1. **The four deterministic repairs** preprocessing runs
20	   ([`worker.mjs`](../../../../packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs)):
21	   - **converge** — rebuild `.claudinite/shared/` to the canon vendor set
22	     ([`apply-vendor-set.mjs`](../../../../vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs)).
23	   - **converge-wiring** — the scheduler workflow + hashed cron, the settings
24	     hooks, and the retired-import removal
25	     ([`converge-wiring.mjs`](../../../../engine/converge-wiring.mjs), and the pack's
26	     [`converge-workflows.mjs`](../../../../packs/claudinite-tasks/converge-workflows.mjs)).
27	   - **declaration-normalization** — the `local/<name>` pack token.
28	   - **mechanical migrations** — aliases / materialize / rewrite
29	     ([`engine/migrations/apply.mjs`](../../../../engine/migrations/apply.mjs)).
30	2. **The escalation gate** — preprocessing requests the agent iff a pending
31	   *agentic* migration note exists, **or** the converge changed something and
32	   `check_the_world` is **not green**.
33	
34	## Finding — the classification of all 59 checks
35	
36	Full per-check classification was produced by enumerating every rule module
37	(`packs/*`, `packs/*/skills/*`, `engine/checks/`, `.claudinite/local/packs/*`).
38	The shape of the result:
39	
40	- **Subsumed by a deterministic repair — 2.**
41	  - `scheduler-workflow-shape` → **converge-wiring** rewrites that exact workflow
42	    to the vendored stub with the repo's hashed cron.
43	  - `cer/release-workflows` → the `chrome-release-vendoring` migration's
44	    materialize/rewrite self-heals the vendored reusable-workflows/actions drift.
45	    (Its orchestrator name/schedule/token assertions are one-time adoption
46	    authoring, not recurring nightly drift.)
47	- **No check maps to converge, declaration-normalization, retired-import, or
48	  hook-registration.** Conformance rules target the consumer's **authored**
49	  surface, never the vendored mount content or the wiring registrations. So those
50	  repairs run **unconditionally** in preprocessing with no gate needed — there is
51	  nothing for a check to have caught.
52	- **Needs-judgment — the rest (~55).** Genuine decisions: code quality, author
53	  doc/reference integrity, file placement, security, process discipline, pack /
54	  release / product-wiki authoring. These are exactly what *should* summon an
55	  agent, not be auto-edited by a mechanical converge.
56	
57	## The load-bearing subtlety — `check_the_world` ≠ every check
58	
59	The escalation gate runs **`check_the_world`** (world scope). It does **not** run
60	**8 work-scoped rules**, which run only in `check_the_work` against a session's
61	diff/transcript:
62	
63	`reference-integrity`, `comment-classification`, `task-lifecycle`,
64	`squash-merge-history`, `feature-requirements-first`, `node/earn-each-dependency`,
65	`cer/permission-added-store-issue`, `google-client-id-single-origin`
66	(plus `promote-scope`, a CI-only gate on the growth-promote branch).
67	
68	So the gate is **blind** to those 8. Are they a silent regression? **No** — and
69	this is the crux of why the agentless night is sound:
70	
71	> A work-scoped check judges a **session's change**, not standing repo state. On an
72	> agentless night there is no agent session, and preprocessing's only change is the
73	> **mechanical converge** — vendored canon files (already clean) plus the stamp.
74	> That diff makes none of the moves these checks police:
75	> - `reference-integrity` / `markdown` — the converge writes vendored files, which
76	>   carry no broken author links; pre-existing dangling links in *unchanged* author
77	>   files were never in a work-scoped check's view (or the old align's), so leaving
78	>   them is not new.
79	> - `task-lifecycle` / `squash-merge-history` — baselining's delivery is one
80	>   mechanical commit that `Refs` the tracking issue on the maintenance PR, correct
81	>   by construction.
82	> - `earn-each-dependency` / `permission-added` / `google-client-id` /
83	>   `comment-classification` / `feature-requirements-first` — each fires on a
84	>   specific authored act (adding a dep, a permission, a client-id literal, replying
85	>   to the owner, a feature commit) that a mechanical converge never performs.
86	
87	Every check that judges **standing repo state** (the drift a nightly refresh is
88	meant to catch) **is** world-scoped and therefore **is** in the gate. The
89	work-scoped exclusions judge changes the converge does not make. **No silent
90	regression.**
91	
92	## Conclusion
93	
94	**It is safe to drive baselining's common-night model toward `null`.** The
95	escalation gate (`check_the_world` green **and** no pending agentic note) covers
96	every standing-repo judgment check; the deterministic repairs cover the mount,
97	wiring, normalization, and mechanical migrations (none of which a check guards);
98	and the work-scoped checks the gate omits judge session changes a mechanical
99	converge never makes. Until the model is actually flipped to `null`, the gate is
100	already the operative safety net — a converge left non-green escalates today.
101	
102	## Backlog — mechanize to reduce needless escalation (non-blocking)
103	
104	Three **world-scoped** needs-judgment checks have a genuinely **rote** fix. Today a
105	repo failing one escalates to an agent (safe, but wasteful). Making each an
106	additional deterministic repair would keep more nights agentless:
107	
108	- `catalog-completeness` — regenerate `packs/README.md` entries from the pack tree.
109	- `generated-merge-driver` — add the known `.gitattributes` `merge=ours` line for a
110	  GENERATED file that lacks it.
111	- `cer/version-sync` — set `package.json` version := the manifest version.
112	
113	None blocks the null-model flip; each is an incremental way to shrink the set of
114	nights that need an agent at all.
